case1.title: CASE 1: PERSISTENT LOWER BACK PAIN
case1.raw_text: My father has had persistent lower back pain for about three weeks. It gets worse when he stands for a long time. He has no breathing difficulty, severe bleeding, loss of consciousness, or major recent injury. We have not consulted a doctor yet. What kind of medical professional should we see, what warning signs should we watch for, and what should we do next?
case1.situation_brief: The citizen reports that his father is experiencing persistent lower back pain for three weeks, which worsens with prolonged standing. The primary threat is the potential development of serious spinal pathology, indicated by red‑flag symptoms such as leg weakness, numbness, or bowel/bladder dysfunction. No medical consultation has been sought yet, and the father has not taken any specific actions beyond coping with the discomfort. The coordinator should arrange for a prompt referral to an appropriate medical professional (primary care physician, orthopaedic specialist, or physiotherapist) and provide guidance on monitoring red‑flag signs.

triage.primary_concern:
Adult patient presenting with persistent lower back pain for three weeks duration. Mechanism: gradual onset, pain worsens with prolonged standing, no recent injury. Current status: stable. Key concerns: 
- Possible underlying spinal pathology (e.g., disc issue) 
- Monitor for red-flag symptoms: leg weakness, numbness, bowel/bladder incontinence, fever, unexplained weight loss
interventions: Seek professional evaluation: Identify underlying cause and appropriate management — Delay may allow condition to worsen or miss serious pathology — Visit a primary care physician, orthopaedic specialist, or physiotherapist; if none available, use telemedicine services for assessment.

Monitor red-flag signs: Early detection of serious condition — Missing may lead to irreversible neurologic damage — Observe for leg weakness, numbness, bowel/bladder incontinence, fever, or severe unrelenting pain; if any appear, call emergency services (108).

Use over-the-counter analgesics as per label: Alleviate discomfort — Untreated pain may affect mobility and quality of life — Take acetaminophen or NSAID following package instructions, ensuring no allergy or contraindication.

golden_window.consequence_of_delay: Routine medical evaluation recommended without artificial deadline

case2.title: CASE 2: EARACHE AND DIZZINESS
case2.raw_text: My sister has had mild persistent ear pain and dizziness for 4 days after a cold. No fever, no discharge, no confusion, no sudden hearing loss. We haven't seen a doctor yet. Who should we consult and what precautions should we take?
case2.situation_brief: The sister is suffering mild ear pain and dizziness for four days after a cold. The most urgent threat is the potential development of a middle‑ear infection or worsening symptoms if red‑flag signs appear. No medical consultation has been sought yet and no self‑treatment has been performed. The coordinator should facilitate arranging a prompt primary‑care or ENT appointment and provide clear guidance on monitoring and ear‑care precautions.

triage.primary_concern:
Age not specified year old patient presenting with mild ear pain and dizziness for 4 days duration. Mechanism: post-viral upper respiratory infection. Current status: conscious, stable. Key concerns:
- Persistent ear pain
- Dizziness
- Potential middle ear infection
- Need for ENT evaluation
interventions: Consult healthcare professional: to assess for possible otitis media or eustachian tube dysfunction — delayed diagnosis may lead to worsening infection or hearing loss — schedule an appointment with a primary care physician or ENT specialist; if unable to obtain an appointment promptly, visit the nearest clinic or hospital outpatient department for evaluation

Monitor for red-flag symptoms: watch for fever, worsening pain, sudden hearing loss, ear discharge, or vomiting — missing red flags may allow progression to acute infection or complications — keep a daily symptom log and seek immediate medical care if any of these signs develop

Keep ear dry and avoid self‑cleaning: to prevent secondary infection or irritation — water or objects in the ear can cause otitis externa or trauma — use a cotton ball coated with petroleum jelly while showering and refrain from inserting objects into the ear canal

golden_window.consequence_of_delay: Routine medical evaluation recommended without artificial deadline

emergency_contacts.name: National Ambulance
emergency_contacts.when_to_call: if severe ear pain, high fever, sudden hearing loss, vomiting, or worsening dizziness occurs

immediate_actions.action: Schedule an appointment with a primary care physician or ENT specialist for evaluation
Monitor for red‑flag symptoms (fever, worsening pain, hearing loss, discharge, vomiting) and seek immediate care if any appear
Keep the ear dry; use a cotton ball with petroleum jelly while showering and avoid inserting objects
Maintain a daily symptom log noting pain level, dizziness, temperature, and any new signs
